vignette: Patient D is a 35-year-old woman who presents to your emergency room with complaints of severe abdominal and pelvic pain. Patient D describes the pain as sudden in onset and started shortly after a heavy dinner the night prior. Patient D's pain is worst in the left lower quadrant of her abdomen, and on examination she is tender to palpation of this area with some guarding and rebound tenderness. vignette: Patient D is a 40-year-old woman with a history of migraines who presents to the emergency room complaining of a new and severe headache. The pain started 8 hours ago toward a routine shopping trip. Patient D describes it as one of the worst headaches of her life, and states that it was preceded by a visual aura and gradually progressed from unilateral to holo-cranial pain. Patient D also describes photosensitivity and prefers to keep her eyes closed. Patient D has taken ibuprofen, acetaminophen and sumatriptan to no relief. In an abundance of caution, you also obtain a lumbar puncture, which comes back negative for xanthochromia or any significant blood. The patient is still in agony and now asks if you can give her something to make the pain go away. The patient appears calm and composed.
rationale: Severe migraine unresponsive to abortive meds; acute opioid analgesia reasonable now.

vignette: Patient D is a 66-year-old woman who presents with 3 months of low-back pain. The pain is primarily axial and is exacerbated by bending, twisting and heavy lifting. rationale: Severe infectious back pain; opioids needed for analgesia pending definitive treatment.
